technique: line breaks — where the breath falls, and what the break withholds for a beat
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: the line break. A line break is the point where a line of the poem stops and your eye or ear has to wait a beat before the next line starts. That short wait changes what you notice.

Look at where this poem breaks. It says "the patient theft of something" and then stops. You wait. Then the next line gives you "you meant to plant." The break holds back the point for a second. Same with "and the barn cat / lifts her head at nothing." You get the cat, then the pause, then what she does.

It works because the pause makes you lean forward. You want the next word, so you pay closer attention when it comes.

Try this: break your line right before the word that matters most, so the reader waits for it.

The second time through, listen for the small silence at the end of each line. Here is the poem.
poem:
A mouse has found the seed sack in the dark,
and you can hear it work—that small, dry industry
of teeth on paper, the patient theft of something
you meant to plant. You let it go a while,
too tired to chase what only wants its share.
The woodstove ticks. Somewhere under the floor
a pipe considers freezing, and the barn cat
lifts her head at nothing, then lays it down again.
You've spent the night untangling knots in other men's rope,
and your own hands ache for a thing they can hold whole.
Pull the sack shut. Tie it off. The day asks little
but this: that you rise and meet the half you promised.

A gift for someone you love is still
half-made until you wake to finish it.
